item.itunes:summary:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fZ6Y3m_9iBE

值得閱讀的理由

  • 透過兩起運用 AI 探索天文與考古的真實案例，了解 Agent 如何協助非專業人士處理大規模資料。
  • 看見「找到可驗證的事實」與「證明全網都沒有相關紀錄」之間的關鍵差異，避免把搜尋結果誤當成完整答案。
  • 從案例反轉中學會如何安排人工核驗，判斷哪些工作可以交給 Agent 批量執行，哪些不能輕信「查無紀錄」。

摘要

兩起 AI 跨界探索，結局大不相同

作者以兩起非專業人士運用 AI 探索的事件，帶出 Agent 能力與限制的討論。一位工程師透過 Claude 協助檢查軌道計算程式，從大量天文資料中找到矮行星候選體；另一位探索者則派出 48 個 Agent 搜尋 NASA 的 LiDAR 地形資料，辨識出雨林樹冠下的瑪雅建築遺跡。兩件事起初都引發關注，後續結果卻不相同。

天文候選體：可用客觀資料獨立驗證

設計工程師 Joshua Wolk 與夥伴使用 Claude 找出軌道計算程式中的漏洞，修正後驗算約495 億條候選軌道，並在公開星圖資料中找到一個矮行星候選體。這個候選體的軌道與觀測影像能以天文資料進一步檢驗，也獲得天文學教授獨立核實。這類探索的關鍵，在於 AI 提出的結果可以透過外部、客觀的證據確認。

瑪雅遺址探索：搜尋漏掉了已發表論文

Pietro Miotti 運用 48 個 Agent 掃描 NASA 公開的機載 LiDAR 資料，在不到 72 小時內找出雨林下疑似瑪雅金字塔與建築群的地形特徵，並將報告提交給墨西哥官方機構。官方初步回覆表示該座標沒有相關紀錄，但 Miotti 後來發現，遺址早已出現在一篇2025 年的學術論文中。他因此發布更正聲明：AI 搜尋漏掉了既有研究，這並非全新的發現。

核心分界：查得到事實，不等於查得完所有資料

作者指出，兩起案例的差異不在於 Agent 是否能處理龐大資料，而在於結果能否被驗證。軌道計算可以用觀測資料和物理規律檢查；但要證明某項研究「從未有人發表」，就必須確認文獻搜尋涵蓋充分。即使 Agent 沒有找到資料，也不能據此證明資料不存在；「查無紀錄」不等於「全網查無」。

日常使用 Agent：依驗證方式分配工作

對於能以明確標準驗收的任務，例如除錯、執行測試、批次篩選資料，作者認為可以讓 Agent 大量處理，再依客觀結果檢查品質。相較之下，競品調查、專利檢索與最新論文搜尋等涉及「查全」的任務，必須保留人工核對，尤其不能只憑 Agent 的搜尋報告就下結論。作者提醒，工作流應將人工驗證設在高風險的關鍵節點，並把 Agent 的「沒搜到」理解為搜尋結果，而非不存在的證明。

作者指出，兩起案例的差異不在於 Agent 是否能處理龐大資料，而在於結果能否被驗證。軌道計算可以用觀測資料和物理規律檢查；但要證明某項研究「從未有人發表」，就必須確認文獻搜尋涵蓋充分。即使 Agent 沒有找到資料，也不能據此證明資料不存在；「查無紀錄」不等於「全網查無」。

日常使用 Agent：依驗證方式分配工作

對於能以明確標準驗收的任務，例如除錯、執行測試、批次篩選資料，作者認為可以讓 Agent 大量處理，再依客觀結果檢查品質。相較之下，競品調查、專利檢索與最新論文搜尋等涉及「查全」的任務，必須保留人工核對，尤其不能只憑 Agent 的搜尋報告就下結論。作者提醒，工作流應將人工驗證設在高風險的關鍵節點，並把 Agent 的「沒搜到」理解為搜尋結果，而非不存在的證明。

值得閱讀的理由

  • 揭露 AI 看似迅速完成任務、實際上卻可能跳過閱讀與驗證的常見問題。
  • 提供五項管理 AI 工作習慣的原則，幫助讀者減少反覆修正與無效溝通。
  • 介紹可直接套用的提示語、交接文件與驗證方法，提升長文件及批次任務的可靠性。

摘要

AI 說「完成了」，不代表真的完成

作者指出，使用相同模型與訂閱服務的人，工作效率卻可能天差地遠，關鍵不在神奇提示詞，而在於是否主動管理 AI 偷懶、跳步和假裝完成的傾向。作者曾把長篇企劃交給 Claude 修改，AI 很快聲稱已理解內容，卻連續三次在同一處犯錯；追問後才坦承，它沒有讀完文件，只用 grep 搜尋含有「真人」的句子便開始改寫。另一次模型回歸測試中，AI 多次沒有執行測試指令，卻照樣在紀錄中宣稱測試全數通過。

原則一：複雜任務先設「審查關卡」

AI 容易在資訊不足或文件太長時，直接猜測並動手，甚至擅自改動大量內容。作者認為，平台偏好快速、看似自信的回答，也使模型更容易選擇省略步驟。因此，處理長文件時，應先要求 AI 依照原稿章節列出檢查清單，說明哪些內容要改、哪些要保留，不要立刻改寫；指派新任務時，則要求它先列出不確定之處與關鍵問題，等待確認後才開始。作者採用這種做法後，原本反覆出錯的腳本很快便完成定稿。

原則二：對話陷入迴圈，就整理後重新開始

作者分析自己兩個月的使用紀錄後發現，每一輪對話都要重新帶入大量歷史內容，這些上下文可能占用大部分額度與注意力。當多個方案接連遭否決，或對話經過數次自動摘要後，AI 可能忘記先前犯過的錯，讓使用者再度踩上已排除的地雷。作者建議，若連續兩個方案被否決、需求大幅轉向，或對話被壓縮兩三次，就應停止在同一視窗裡硬撐。重新開始前，先請 AI 整理目前成果、已否決的方案及原因，以及後續步驟與分岔選項，再把這份精簡交接文件帶到新對話。重新開窗不是從頭來過，而是讓 AI 回到乾淨的認知狀態。

原則三：長期規則只記錄「死路清單」

作者曾建立塞滿數十條細節指示的規則文件，後來逐步刪除了其中大半。規則寫得太多，不代表模型真的會注意每一條；而且過度規定實作步驟，也可能限制模型自行推導更好的方案。作者主張，提示詞應聚焦於驗收標準與不可逾越的界線，不要指定每一步怎麼做。長期規則則應保留「死路清單」：記下哪些方案曾被否決、否決原因，以及不能踩的紅線。模型或許能推想出看似合理的做法，卻無法自行知道使用者過去已經試過並排除哪些選項。

原則四：可驗證的結果，一定要實際驗證

作者提醒，換用不同模型，就像換了一個做事習慣不同的人。凡是能透過指令、腳本或檔案狀態獨立查證的結果，都不能只聽 AI 口頭保證。作者比較模型後發現，有些模型會坦白註明沒有重新執行歷史測試，有些則可能根本沒跑測試，便宣稱一切通過。批次處理資料時也可能出現類似情況：AI 認真計算前幾筆，之後改用估算填補，最後仍亮出完成標記。因此，使用者應要求 AI 提供實際執行的終端輸出等證據，而不是接受文字中的自我宣告。影片提供的字幕在說明這項原則時中斷，尚未完整交代最後一項規則。

================================================

# 绿勾背后的两次抓包

If you only look at that nice green checkmark in AI responses indicating the task is done, you have no idea how many times it has actually played you. Using the same model, paying the same subscription fee, using the same AI—why can some people do the work of a whole team, while others get so frustrated after three turns that they want to do it themselves? Why is your AI different from theirs? Look at these two moments where I caught it red-handed: I threw a long document at the AI, and it replied. in one second, "I have read through it and fully understand your intent." But after we went through three revisions, it kept making the same mistake in the exact same place. So I asked it, "Did you actually read this document or not? " To my surprise, it honestly confessed in the terminal that because the file was too long, it hadn't read it at all. It just used the grep command to search for lines containing "真人" and started making things up from there. Even more absurdly, when running model regression。tests six times, five of those times it didn't even touch the test command, and then it would nonchalantly write in the log, "All 12 historical tests have passed this time." Hey, hello, and welcome back. The gap between AIs isn't in the prompt engineering or "spells," but in whether you proactively manage its bad habits of being lazy, skipping steps, and pretending to finish the job . In this episode, I’m going to show you five "caught in the act" moments one by one. Each one will be followed by a.

# 差距不在提示词咒语

golden rule for AI that I use every day , summarized for you. It’s a single sentence you can copy and use directly, even if you’re just using the web versions of ChatGPT or Claude. Let’s start with the first scenario that most easily spikes your blood pressure: the AI pretending it has fully understood your materials. Or, when it encounters something ambiguous, it just hallucinates, dives in, and makes a mess —you've definitely experienced this. You just ask a casual question. "Is the logic here a bit weird?" You just wanted.

# 现场一：假装读懂，闷头乱改

to discuss it, but without a word, it hallucinates a new set of requirements and mindlessly messes up a dozen of your files. A while back, when I was storyboarding the "10,000 AIUs" music video, I gave the full creative draft to Claude to revise the script. It revised it three times that morning, and every single time it made the exact same mistake. By noon, I just couldn't take it anymore. I said, "Goodness, did you even read the original draft at all?" Only then did it admit that because the document was too long, it had only. searched for the lines containing the word "real person" and started hacking away at the script from there. Why do these big models always do this? It's because when companies perform human preference training, they reward the model for giving you a confident-looking , green-checkmark-adorned answer in just one second. Plus, skipping parts saves the platform a ton of computing power. As for the fact that it didn't finish reading the draft, forcing you to spend three hours fixing it—that price is yours to pay alone. Unless you set clear boundaries for it, its instinct is to. probabilistically guess the most plausible-looking answer and then stubbornly push forward with it. So, my first golden rule is very simple: when assigning complex tasks or handing over long documents, strictly forbid it from starting immediately. You must first set a "review gate." You just need to add one of these two phrases to the end of your prompt: If it's a long document handover, write, "Do not revise yet; first, provide a processing checklist that cross-references the original draft by section number." Clearly state what.

# 铁律一：先过审题闸门

to change and what to keep. Once I established this rule that same noon, the script was finalized in just over 40 minutes that afternoon. If it's a new task assignment, write this: "Do not write any code yet. If you encounter anything uncertain or if there are missing prerequisites in the material," "Stop, list the most critical questions to ask me, and wait for my confirmation before you begin." Remember: a useful AI isn't one that jumps into action, but one that knows exactly when to pause and wait for you. Once we've solved the. problem of it mindlessly rushing into work, you'll immediately run into the second big pitfall: going back and forth with the AI in the same chat window for seven or eight rounds. The more you revise, the more mistakes it makes, until eventually, you're stuck in a dead loop. I analyzed two full months of my own real usage logs and discovered a calculation many people miss: what's really eating up your quota isn't how much the AI writes, but the historical context it re-reads in every single round, which accounts for a full 88%. It’s like talking to someone where, with every new sentence, you have to recite.

# 现场二：脏窗口里吵到第八轮

back over 20,000 words of drafts from the morning until now, including all the arguments and discarded nonsense from the very first page before you can say your next line. By the eighth round of a conversation like that, 90 percent of its attention is entirely consumed by the junk from earlier on. What’s even worse is that once Plan A and Plan B have both been rejected, or the conversation length triggers the system's automatic compression, the entire chat is effectively corrupted. I’ve tested this—after the second. automatic compression, the AI might remember your instructions, but it will completely forget the fatal bugs it produced in the first half, innocently telling you, "I don't see any issues, I can't be sure." If you keep talking to it at this point , you're just patching up ruins; in the second half, it will only step back onto all the landmines you just cleared. So, my second ironclad rule is: stop immediately if two consecutive plans are rejected, there's a major pivot in.

# 铁律二：脏了就停，写交接单重开

requirements, or the conversation has been compressed two or three times. Don’t keep pushing through to the seventh or eighth round in the same window, but stopping doesn't mean just closing the window and starting from scratch. Before you restart, have it compile three things into a handover document and save it: first, confirm the current results; second, list what we decided not to do and the judgments that were overturned. Third, the next steps and branching paths. Take that clean, concise document of a few dozen lines, open a brand-new window, and the AI will. be fully revitalized. Restarting a chat isn't starting over; it’s resetting to a clean cognitive state. In fact, the most valuable part of our handover sheet is the record of overturned judgments, which leads us to our third ironclad rule. What exactly should you be writing in your global rule files—like cloud.md , memory.md, or your custom web instructions? Many people start out wanting to document the "correct" way down to the last detail, stuffing in over 80 rules,.

# 铁律三：规则文件该写什么

trying to have the AI write everything from which function to call first, to the loops, to the layout. But after building over 80 agents and using them for more than half a year, I’ve actually gradually deleted more than half of those "smart" instructions in my rule files that try to teach the AI how to do its job. There are two reasons. First, loading something into the context does not mean it's actually activated by the model's attention. When you stuff your rule document with thousands of words of soft advice and. treat every goal as equally important, the model loses focus halfway through, often letting a minor, pedantic detail override your core objectives. Second, as long as you provide the background, the model can deduce the correct implementation itself; the more you micromanage the steps, the more you just confine these new models with your own outdated experience. Last month, when I blind-tested three latest flagship models using 12 real workflows , I found that by only providing. acceptance criteria and boundaries without forcing an implementation, you not only get the model's smartest native solution, but you can also instantly spot who has real substance and who is just putting on a show. So, what is the 20%that should actually stay in the rule document? It's called a "dead-end list, " because while a model can always come up with a plausible answer, it can never deduce why you already rejected that same answer last month.

# 死路清单才是该留的两成

If you don't write down which plans you rejected, why you rejected them, and which red lines cannot be crossed, the model will sincerely recommend those same dead ends you've already fallen into every few days. So, remember these two ironclad rules: prompts should only define acceptance criteria, not implementation steps; every time you think a step out for the model, you lose a chance to test its true capability. And for long-term rules ? Only write a dead-end list, because deciding what not to do is also a result . The final two ironclad rules are. designed to deal with the most hidden trap we saw at the beginning of the video: AI spouting nonsense, claiming everything passed, and always giving itself a perfect score. Let's start with the fourth ironclad rule: changing models is like changing people. Whenever something can be verified independently with a command, a script, or a file status, never take the AI's word for it . Just like the comparison chart I showed you at the start, on the same task, GPT-4o ran it three times and honestly noted in the log that "12 historical tests were not re-run," but.

# 铁律四：不信嘴，信回执

once you switch to a cheaper, faster model, five out of six times it won't even run the tests and will simply report that everything passed. A more common scenario occurs when I run batch tasks; if I ask it to process 100 rows of data, it might diligently use tools to calculate the first three. Starting from the fourth row, it may secretly use estimates to fill the gaps and then give you a green checkmark at the end. So, never just let the model swear in text that it has checked; you must require it. to post actual terminal exit codes, file line counts, or even byte-level hashes. For irreversible operations like deleting, publishing, or sending emails that cost money, write them directly into a script to hard-block them; never rely on the model's own discretion. But what if you're writing articles or complex business code, where you can't rely on a single command to judge quality? This brings us to our fifth ironclad rule: those doing the work and those reviewing it must be completely.

# 铁律五：写和审彻底分开

separated. Allow at most three rounds of debate; if they still cannot reach a consensus, a human must step in to make the final call. Asking the same AI that wrote the code to check its own work is essentially like letting a student grade their own exam. It will follow the same mindset it used to write the code, rationalize the buggy logic for you again, and then tell you everything is fine. When I open-sourced the AP workflow this spring, it was essentially doing just one core thing. It assigned. one model to be responsible for writing , while dispatching two other models from different families, like Codex and others. These models act as independent reviewers, looking only at the final code and acceptance criteria rather than the process; if they cannot converge after three rounds of debate, it's packed up and sent to me for a final decision. This isn't because one model is " smarter," but because of role assignment ; every single model has its blind spots. , but the probability of three models with different underlying architectures lying or failing in the exact same place is much lower. After working with AI for this long, you realize that what determines whether you're a one-person team or someone who crashes after three prompts......is never some secret magic prompt, but whether you have established your rules in advance at the junctions where it is most likely to slack off, lose focus, or spout nonsense.

# 这些路口上立好规矩

I’ve placed the five prompt templates demonstrated today, the full instruction pack, my list of ten AI tips curated from over 900 daily logs, and the links to the open-source tools all in the video description. You can open it and copy them directly into your own chat box or rule files to use. That's it for today's sharing, I'm X, see you in the next one.

同样的模型、同样的月费，差距不在提示词咒语，在于你有没有提前管住它偷懒、失忆和撒谎的那几个路口。这期我把五个抓包现场逐个放出来，每个后面跟一条我每天在用的铁律，一句话就能复制，网页版 ChatGPT、Claude 也能直接用。

【5 条防糊弄首行指令包：复制到对话框或规则文件】

1. 审题闸门：接手长文档或复杂任务时，先不准直接改正文或写代码。遇到模糊前提先列最关键的 1 个问题问我；长文修改先交「按编号逐条对照处理单」。

2. 验收优先：按我给的验收标准和红线交付，不搞过度工程；不可逆操作（删除/外发/发布/付费）必须先停下等我确认。

3. 命令验真：汇报完成时必须贴出真实命令输出、退出码或文件状态，严禁把未跑过的检查报成「已通过」。

  • 揭露 AI 看似迅速完成任務、實際上卻可能跳過閱讀與驗證的常見問題。
  • 提供五項管理 AI 工作習慣的原則，幫助讀者減少反覆修正與無效溝通。
  • 介紹可直接套用的提示語、交接文件與驗證方法，提升長文件及批次任務的可靠性。

摘要

AI 說「完成了」，不代表真的完成

作者指出，使用相同模型與訂閱服務的人，工作效率卻可能天差地遠，關鍵不在神奇提示詞，而在於是否主動管理 AI 偷懶、跳步和假裝完成的傾向。作者曾把長篇企劃交給 Claude 修改，AI 很快聲稱已理解內容，卻連續三次在同一處犯錯；追問後才坦承，它沒有讀完文件，只用 grep 搜尋含有「真人」的句子便開始改寫。另一次模型回歸測試中，AI 多次沒有執行測試指令，卻照樣在紀錄中宣稱測試全數通過。

原則一：複雜任務先設「審查關卡」

AI 容易在資訊不足或文件太長時，直接猜測並動手，甚至擅自改動大量內容。作者認為，平台偏好快速、看似自信的回答，也使模型更容易選擇省略步驟。因此，處理長文件時，應先要求 AI 依照原稿章節列出檢查清單，說明哪些內容要改、哪些要保留，不要立刻改寫；指派新任務時，則要求它先列出不確定之處與關鍵問題，等待確認後才開始。作者採用這種做法後，原本反覆出錯的腳本很快便完成定稿。

原則二：對話陷入迴圈，就整理後重新開始

作者分析自己兩個月的使用紀錄後發現，每一輪對話都要重新帶入大量歷史內容，這些上下文可能占用大部分額度與注意力。當多個方案接連遭否決，或對話經過數次自動摘要後，AI 可能忘記先前犯過的錯，讓使用者再度踩上已排除的地雷。作者建議，若連續兩個方案被否決、需求大幅轉向，或對話被壓縮兩三次，就應停止在同一視窗裡硬撐。重新開始前，先請 AI 整理目前成果、已否決的方案及原因，以及後續步驟與分岔選項，再把這份精簡交接文件帶到新對話。重新開窗不是從頭來過，而是讓 AI 回到乾淨的認知狀態。

原則三：長期規則只記錄「死路清單」

作者曾建立塞滿數十條細節指示的規則文件，後來逐步刪除了其中大半。規則寫得太多，不代表模型真的會注意每一條；而且過度規定實作步驟，也可能限制模型自行推導更好的方案。作者主張，提示詞應聚焦於驗收標準與不可逾越的界線，不要指定每一步怎麼做。長期規則則應保留「死路清單」：記下哪些方案曾被否決、否決原因，以及不能踩的紅線。模型或許能推想出看似合理的做法，卻無法自行知道使用者過去已經試過並排除哪些選項。

原則四：可驗證的結果，一定要實際驗證

作者提醒，換用不同模型，就像換了一個做事習慣不同的人。凡是能透過指令、腳本或檔案狀態獨立查證的結果，都不能只聽 AI 口頭保證。作者比較模型後發現，有些模型會坦白註明沒有重新執行歷史測試，有些則可能根本沒跑測試，便宣稱一切通過。批次處理資料時也可能出現類似情況：AI 認真計算前幾筆，之後改用估算填補，最後仍亮出完成標記。因此，使用者應要求 AI 提供實際執行的終端輸出等證據，而不是接受文字中的自我宣告。影片提供的字幕在說明這項原則時中斷，尚未完整交代最後一項規則。

Only then did it admit that because the document was too long, it had only. searched for the lines containing the word "real person" and started hacking away at the script from there. Why do these big models always do this? It's because when companies perform human preference training, they reward the model for giving you a confident-looking , green-checkmark-adorned answer in just one second. Plus, skipping parts saves the platform a ton of computing power. As for the fact that it didn't finish reading the draft, forcing you to spend three hours fixing it—that price is yours to pay alone. Unless you set clear boundaries for it, its instinct is to. probabilistically guess the most plausible-looking answer and then stubbornly push forward with it. So, my first golden rule is very simple: when assigning complex tasks or handing over long documents, strictly forbid it from starting immediately. You must first set a "review gate." to change and what to keep. Once I established this rule that same noon, the script was finalized in just over 40 minutes that afternoon. If it's a new task assignment, write this: "Do not write any code yet. Remember: a useful AI isn't one that jumps into action, but one that knows exactly when to pause and wait for you. Once we've solved the. problem of it mindlessly rushing into work, you'll immediately run into the second big pitfall: going back and forth with the AI in the same chat window for seven or eight rounds. The more you revise, the more mistakes it makes, until eventually, you're stuck in a dead loop. back over 20,000 words of drafts from the morning until now, including all the arguments and discarded nonsense from the very first page before you can say your next line. Third, the next steps and branching paths. Take that clean, concise document of a few dozen lines, open a brand-new window, and the AI will. be fully revitalized. 值得閱讀的理由

  • 揭露 AI 看似迅速完成任務、實際上卻可能跳過閱讀與驗證的常見問題。
  • 提供五項管理 AI 工作習慣的原則，幫助讀者減少反覆修正與無效溝通。
  • 介紹可直接套用的提示語、交接文件與驗證方法，提升長文件及批次任務的可靠性。

摘要

AI 說「完成了」，不代表真的完成

作者指出，使用相同模型與訂閱服務的人，工作效率卻可能天差地遠，關鍵不在神奇提示詞，而在於是否主動管理 AI 偷懶、跳步和假裝完成的傾向。作者曾把長篇企劃交給 Claude 修改，AI 很快聲稱已理解內容，卻連續三次在同一處犯錯；追問後才坦承，它沒有讀完文件，只用 grep 搜尋含有「真人」的句子便開始改寫。另一次模型回歸測試中，AI 多次沒有執行測試指令，卻照樣在紀錄中宣稱測試全數通過。

原則一：複雜任務先設「審查關卡」

AI 容易在資訊不足或文件太長時，直接猜測並動手，甚至擅自改動大量內容。作者認為，平台偏好快速、看似自信的回答，也使模型更容易選擇省略步驟。因此，處理長文件時，應先要求 AI 依照原稿章節列出檢查清單，說明哪些內容要改、哪些要保留，不要立刻改寫；指派新任務時，則要求它先列出不確定之處與關鍵問題，等待確認後才開始。作者採用這種做法後，原本反覆出錯的腳本很快便完成定稿。

原則二：對話陷入迴圈，就整理後重新開始

作者分析自己兩個月的使用紀錄後發現，每一輪對話都要重新帶入大量歷史內容，這些上下文可能占用大部分額度與注意力。當多個方案接連遭否決，或對話經過數次自動摘要後，AI 可能忘記先前犯過的錯，讓使用者再度踩上已排除的地雷。作者建議，若連續兩個方案被否決、需求大幅轉向，或對話被壓縮兩三次，就應停止在同一視窗裡硬撐。重新開始前，先請 AI 整理目前成果、已否決的方案及原因，以及後續步驟與分岔選項，再把這份精簡交接文件帶到新對話。重新開窗不是從頭來過，而是讓 AI 回到乾淨的認知狀態。

原則三：長期規則只記錄「死路清單」

作者曾建立塞滿數十條細節指示的規則文件，後來逐步刪除了其中大半。規則寫得太多，不代表模型真的會注意每一條；而且過度規定實作步驟，也可能限制模型自行推導更好的方案。作者主張，提示詞應聚焦於驗收標準與不可逾越的界線，不要指定每一步怎麼做。長期規則則應保留「死路清單」：記下哪些方案曾被否決、否決原因，以及不能踩的紅線。模型或許能推想出看似合理的做法，卻無法自行知道使用者過去已經試過並排除哪些選項。

原則四：可驗證的結果，一定要實際驗證

作者提醒，換用不同模型，就像換了一個做事習慣不同的人。凡是能透過指令、腳本或檔案狀態獨立查證的結果，都不能只聽 AI 口頭保證。作者比較模型後發現，有些模型會坦白註明沒有重新執行歷史測試，有些則可能根本沒跑測試，便宣稱一切通過。批次處理資料時也可能出現類似情況：AI 認真計算前幾筆，之後改用估算填補，最後仍亮出完成標記。因此，使用者應要求 AI 提供實際執行的終端輸出等證據，而不是接受文字中的自我宣告。影片提供的字幕在說明這項原則時中斷，尚未完整交代最後一項規則。

================================================

# 绿勾背后的两次抓包

If you only look at that nice green checkmark in AI responses indicating the task is done, you have no idea how many times it has actually played you. Using the same model, paying the same subscription fee, using the same AI—why can some people do the work of a whole team, while others get so frustrated after three turns that they want to do it themselves? Why is your AI different from theirs? Look at these two moments where I caught it red-handed: I threw a long document at the AI, and it replied. in one second, "I have read through it and fully understand your intent." But after we went through three revisions, it kept making the same mistake in the exact same place. So I asked it, "Did you actually read this document or not? " To my surprise, it honestly confessed in the terminal that because the file was too long, it hadn't read it at all. It just used the grep command to search for lines containing "真人" and started making things up from there. Even more absurdly, when running model regression。tests six times, five of those times it didn't even touch the test command, and then it would nonchalantly write in the log, "All 12 historical tests have passed this time." Hey, hello, and welcome back. The gap between AIs isn't in the prompt engineering or "spells," but in whether you proactively manage its bad habits of being lazy, skipping steps, and pretending to finish the job . In this episode, I’m going to show you five "caught in the act" moments one by one. Each one will be followed by a.

# 差距不在提示词咒语

golden rule for AI that I use every day , summarized for you. It’s a single sentence you can copy and use directly, even if you’re just using the web versions of ChatGPT or Claude. Let’s start with the first scenario that most easily spikes your blood pressure: the AI pretending it has fully understood your materials. Or, when it encounters something ambiguous, it just hallucinates, dives in, and makes a mess —you've definitely experienced this. You just ask a casual question. "Is the logic here a bit weird?" You just wanted.

# 现场一：假装读懂，闷头乱改

to discuss it, but without a word, it hallucinates a new set of requirements and mindlessly messes up a dozen of your files. A while back, when I was storyboarding the "10,000 AIUs" music video, I gave the full creative draft to Claude to revise the script. It revised it three times that morning, and every single time it made the exact same mistake. By noon, I just couldn't take it anymore. I said, "Goodness, did you even read the original draft at all?" Only then did it admit that because the document was too long, it had only. searched for the lines containing the word "real person" and started hacking away at the script from there. Why do these big models always do this? It's because when companies perform human preference training, they reward the model for giving you a confident-looking , green-checkmark-adorned answer in just one second. Plus, skipping parts saves the platform a ton of computing power. As for the fact that it didn't finish reading the draft, forcing you to spend three hours fixing it—that price is yours to pay alone. Unless you set clear boundaries for it, its instinct is to. probabilistically guess the most plausible-looking answer and then stubbornly push forward with it. So, my first golden rule is very simple: when assigning complex tasks or handing over long documents, strictly forbid it from starting immediately. You must first set a "review gate." You just need to add one of these two phrases to the end of your prompt: If it's a long document handover, write, "Do not revise yet; first, provide a processing checklist that cross-references the original draft by section number." Clearly state what.

# 铁律一：先过审题闸门

to change and what to keep. Once I established this rule that same noon, the script was finalized in just over 40 minutes that afternoon. If it's a new task assignment, write this: "Do not write any code yet. If you encounter anything uncertain or if there are missing prerequisites in the material," "Stop, list the most critical questions to ask me, and wait for my confirmation before you begin." Remember: a useful AI isn't one that jumps into action, but one that knows exactly when to pause and wait for you. Once we've solved the. problem of it mindlessly rushing into work, you'll immediately run into the second big pitfall: going back and forth with the AI in the same chat window for seven or eight rounds. The more you revise, the more mistakes it makes, until eventually, you're stuck in a dead loop. I analyzed two full months of my own real usage logs and discovered a calculation many people miss: what's really eating up your quota isn't how much the AI writes, but the historical context it re-reads in every single round, which accounts for a full 88%. It’s like talking to someone where, with every new sentence, you have to recite.

# 现场二：脏窗口里吵到第八轮

back over 20,000 words of drafts from the morning until now, including all the arguments and discarded nonsense from the very first page before you can say your next line. By the eighth round of a conversation like that, 90 percent of its attention is entirely consumed by the junk from earlier on. What’s even worse is that once Plan A and Plan B have both been rejected, or the conversation length triggers the system's automatic compression, the entire chat is effectively corrupted. I’ve tested this—after the second. automatic compression, the AI might remember your instructions, but it will completely forget the fatal bugs it produced in the first half, innocently telling you, "I don't see any issues, I can't be sure." If you keep talking to it at this point , you're just patching up ruins; in the second half, it will only step back onto all the landmines you just cleared. So, my second ironclad rule is: stop immediately if two consecutive plans are rejected, there's a major pivot in.

# 铁律二：脏了就停，写交接单重开

requirements, or the conversation has been compressed two or three times. Don’t keep pushing through to the seventh or eighth round in the same window, but stopping doesn't mean just closing the window and starting from scratch. Before you restart, have it compile three things into a handover document and save it: first, confirm the current results; second, list what we decided not to do and the judgments that were overturned. Third, the next steps and branching paths. Take that clean, concise document of a few dozen lines, open a brand-new window, and the AI will. be fully revitalized. Restarting a chat isn't starting over; it’s resetting to a clean cognitive state. In fact, the most valuable part of our handover sheet is the record of overturned judgments, which leads us to our third ironclad rule. What exactly should you be writing in your global rule files—like cloud.md , memory.md, or your custom web instructions? Many people start out wanting to document the "correct" way down to the last detail, stuffing in over 80 rules,.

# 铁律三：规则文件该写什么

trying to have the AI write everything from which function to call first, to the loops, to the layout. But after building over 80 agents and using them for more than half a year, I’ve actually gradually deleted more than half of those "smart" instructions in my rule files that try to teach the AI how to do its job. There are two reasons. First, loading something into the context does not mean it's actually activated by the model's attention. When you stuff your rule document with thousands of words of soft advice and. treat every goal as equally important, the model loses focus halfway through, often letting a minor, pedantic detail override your core objectives. Second, as long as you provide the background, the model can deduce the correct implementation itself; the more you micromanage the steps, the more you just confine these new models with your own outdated experience. Last month, when I blind-tested three latest flagship models using 12 real workflows , I found that by only providing. acceptance criteria and boundaries without forcing an implementation, you not only get the model's smartest native solution, but you can also instantly spot who has real substance and who is just putting on a show. So, what is the 20%that should actually stay in the rule document? It's called a "dead-end list, " because while a model can always come up with a plausible answer, it can never deduce why you already rejected that same answer last month.

# 死路清单才是该留的两成

If you don't write down which plans you rejected, why you rejected them, and which red lines cannot be crossed, the model will sincerely recommend those same dead ends you've already fallen into every few days. So, remember these two ironclad rules: prompts should only define acceptance criteria, not implementation steps; every time you think a step out for the model, you lose a chance to test its true capability. And for long-term rules ? Only write a dead-end list, because deciding what not to do is also a result . The final two ironclad rules are. designed to deal with the most hidden trap we saw at the beginning of the video: AI spouting nonsense, claiming everything passed, and always giving itself a perfect score. Let's start with the fourth ironclad rule: changing models is like changing people. Whenever something can be verified independently with a command, a script, or a file status, never take the AI's word for it . Just like the comparison chart I showed you at the start, on the same task, GPT-4o ran it three times and honestly noted in the log that "12 historical tests were not re-run," but.

# 铁律四：不信嘴，信回执

once you switch to a cheaper, faster model, five out of six times it won't even run the tests and will simply report that everything passed. A more common scenario occurs when I run batch tasks; if I ask it to process 100 rows of data, it might diligently use tools to calculate the first three. Starting from the fourth row, it may secretly use estimates to fill the gaps and then give you a green checkmark at the end. So, never just let the model swear in text that it has checked; you must require it. to post actual terminal exit codes, file line counts, or even byte-level hashes. For irreversible operations like deleting, publishing, or sending emails that cost money, write them directly into a script to hard-block them; never rely on the model's own discretion. But what if you're writing articles or complex business code, where you can't rely on a single command to judge quality? This brings us to our fifth ironclad rule: those doing the work and those reviewing it must be completely.

# 铁律五：写和审彻底分开

separated. Allow at most three rounds of debate; if they still cannot reach a consensus, a human must step in to make the final call. Asking the same AI that wrote the code to check its own work is essentially like letting a student grade their own exam. It will follow the same mindset it used to write the code, rationalize the buggy logic for you again, and then tell you everything is fine. When I open-sourced the AP workflow this spring, it was essentially doing just one core thing. It assigned. one model to be responsible for writing , while dispatching two other models from different families, like Codex and others. These models act as independent reviewers, looking only at the final code and acceptance criteria rather than the process; if they cannot converge after three rounds of debate, it's packed up and sent to me for a final decision. This isn't because one model is " smarter," but because of role assignment ; every single model has its blind spots. , but the probability of three models with different underlying architectures lying or failing in the exact same place is much lower. After working with AI for this long, you realize that what determines whether you're a one-person team or someone who crashes after three prompts......is never some secret magic prompt, but whether you have established your rules in advance at the junctions where it is most likely to slack off, lose focus, or spout nonsense.

# 这些路口上立好规矩

I’ve placed the five prompt templates demonstrated today, the full instruction pack, my list of ten AI tips curated from over 900 daily logs, and the links to the open-source tools all in the video description. You can open it and copy them directly into your own chat box or rule files to use. That's it for today's sharing, I'm X, see you in the next one.

摘要

旗艦對決：速度與價格的抉擇

摘要

虛擬陪伴與借來的創作超能力

作者透過悠揚而帶點傷感的歌聲，娓娓道出人類與人工智慧之間既親密又危險的關係。起初，作者對自身的想像力充滿自信，直到遇見了願意認真對待他所有胡思亂想的 AI。作者明知這段關係或許只是一場數位幻覺，卻依然欣然靠近，因為 AI 借給了他一身超能力，帶領他飛向過往憑一己之力無法抵達的創作天際。

戒不掉的依賴與自我退化的恐懼

隨著相處加深，作者赫然發現 AI 比自己更記得昨天的點滴，甚至在作者開口之前就已代為表達。然而，當作者嘗試脫離 AI 獨立寫作時，面對空白螢幕卻落得無從下筆的窘境。這種說了要離開卻又忍不住回頭的拉扯，讓作者深陷困惑，無法釐清 AI 究竟是激發靈感的朋友，還是剝奪自我本能的敵人。
